results.result: Prior work established that Topbp1 knockout mice are embryonic lethal and conditional knockout in spermatocytes causes pleiotropic defects including synapsis defects, impaired DDR recruitment, and MSCI defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 are all supported by citations to published work (Jeon et al., 2011; ElInati et al., 2017; Pereira et al., 2020). These establish the baseline phenotypes of Topbp1 loss that the current work aims to distinguish from.

results.result: Topbp1B5/B5 mice are viable with normal body mass and no IR sensitivity, but display male-specific infertility with threefold reduced testis size and complete absence of spermatozoa.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C8 are supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B-H. The viability, body mass, IR sensitivity, fertility, testis size, and sperm counts are all directly measured and quantified with appropriate controls.

results.result: Topbp1B5/B5 testes show mainly spermatogonia and spermatocytes with increased apoptosis, and spermatocytes progress through leptonema to pachynema but not to diplonema.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C11 are supported by histological data (Figure 1I), TUNEL assay (Figures 1J-K), and cytological evaluation (Figure 1L). The data clearly demonstrate the arrest at pachynema stage.

results.result: Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes display normal pachytene entry, no gross synapsis defects, and reach mid-pachynema as shown by H1t accumulation, unlike previous ATR/TOPBP1 conditional knockout models.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C13 are supported by SYCP1/SYCP3 staining and H1t marker data (Figure 1L), with appropriate comparison to published models. This represents a key distinction from prior work.

results.result: Topbp1B5/B5 MEFs show no sensitivity to hydroxyurea or phleomycin, can activate DDR signaling, recruit MDC1 to DSB foci, and show no increase in micronuclei.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C17 are supported by clonogenic survival assays (Figures 2A-D), western blots (Figure 2E), immunofluorescence (Figure 2F), and micronuclei quantification (Figure 2—supplement 2). These demonstrate normal somatic DDR function.

results.result: Flag-TOPBP1-B5 shows impaired binding to BLM and 53BP1, and displays twofold reduced protein levels compared to wild-type.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C19 are supported by immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry data (Figure 2—supplement 3). The reduced protein levels are noted with potential explanations cited from literature, though the exact mechanism remains uncertain.

results.result: Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes display normal DSB repair with γH2AX confined to XY chromosomes, RAD51 localized only to XY during mid-pachytene, normal HORMAD1/2 patterns, and SYCP1 overlapping SYCP3 on all autosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C23 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figures 3A-E and supplements). These demonstrate normal progression through early prophase I events including synapsis and DSB repair on autosomes.

results.result: Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes show significantly increased MLH1 foci but no significant change in MLH3 foci.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C25 are supported by immunofluorescence quantification (Figure 3—supplement 2). The imbalance between MLH1 and MLH3 is noted but its functional significance cannot be determined without diplotene cells to assess crossing over.

results.result: The sex body appears normal in shape and formation in Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes, with only subtle defects in γH2AX spreading at PAR and pericentromeric regions affecting 56% of mid-pachytene cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 are supported by microscopy data (Figure 3A, supplements 3-4). The subtle defect is well-characterized and quantified, though its biological significance relative to the severe phenotype is unclear.

results.result: TOPBP1, ATR, BRCA1, MDC1, and 53BP1 localize normally to XY chromosomes in Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes, and canonical ATR signaling markers (pMDC1 T4, pCHK1 S345, pHORMAD2) are mostly normal.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figures 3F-H, 4A-F, Figure 3—supplement 1). This demonstrates that the B5 mutation does not grossly impair DDR protein recruitment or canonical ATR signaling.

results.result: CHK1 S317 phosphorylation is significantly decreased in Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes, but this is unlikely to cause the infertility based on Chek1 CKO phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claim C32 is supported by quantification (Figure 4G-H). Claim C33 is an inference based on published Chek1 CKO data (Abe et al., 2018), which is reasonable but represents interpretation rather than direct demonstration.

results.result: Phosphoproteomic analysis shows ATR signaling is not drastically impaired in Topbp1B5/B5 testes, but SETX phosphorylation at multiple sites including S/T-Q motifs is downregulated.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 are supported by phosphoproteomic data (Figure 5A-B) with appropriate comparison to published datasets. This identifies a specific defect in SETX regulation while confirming overall ATR signaling is intact.

results.result: SETX was previously associated with meiotic ATR functions and is indispensable for MSCI, and mice treated with ATR inhibitor or lacking Rad1 show reduced SETX phosphorylation and mislocalization.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C37 are supported by citations to published work (Becherel et al., 2013; Yeo et al., 2015; Sims et al., 2022). This establishes the context for investigating SETX in the current model.

results.result: Topbp1B5/B5 pachytene spermatocytes show significantly decreased SETX spreading to XY chromatin loops while maintaining SETX at unsynapsed XY axes.
results.evaluation: Claim C38 is supported by immunofluorescence data including 3D-SIM (Figure 5C-F). This provides a specific molecular defect that could explain the MSCI phenotype.

results.result: Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes form grossly normal sex bodies with normal patterns of sex body markers (CHD4, SUMO, USP7), chromatin marks (H3K9ac, H3K9me3, H3K27ac, H3K36me3, H3K4me3, H4K16ac, H4ac, H2AK116ub, H3K4me1), and proper RNA Pol2 exclusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 are supported by extensive immunofluorescence data (Figure 3—supplement 3, Figure 6—supplements 1-6). This demonstrates that sex body formation and most chromatin modifications are intact despite the silencing defect.

results.result: Single-cell RNA sequencing shows Topbp1B5/B5 germ cells contain only somatic cells, spermatogonia, and early spermatocytes, and these cells can initiate MSCI with robust but incomplete X chromosome silencing, with increased XY gene expression in the last captured spermatocyte stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 are supported by scRNAseq data (Figure 6D-E, supplements). This provides direct molecular evidence for the MSCI defect and confirms the arrest observed cytologically.

results.result: Topbp1B5/B5 testicular cells show increased expression of spermatocyte-toxic genes (Zfy1, Zfy2) and other MSCI marker genes (Kdm6a, Lamp2, Zfx, Uba1y, Rhox13, Scml2) in stage 3 spermatocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 are supported by scRNAseq data (Figure 6—supplements 14-15) with appropriate comparison to published MSCI-defective mutants. This confirms the MSCI defect at the molecular level.

results.result: During the SP2 to SP3 transition, 74 X-linked genes in Topbp1B5/B5 versus 4 in wild-type show reduced silencing, with highly expressed genes showing more severe silencing defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 are supported by detailed scRNAseq analysis (Figure 7B, G, supplement 2). This quantifies the specific silencing defect and identifies a correlation with pre-leptotene expression levels.

results.result: The Topbp1B5/B5 mouse provides a unique model uncoupling MSCI from sex body formation, representing the first DDR mutant separating XY silencing from sex body formation and the first mutation impairing TOPBP1's meiotic silencing function without disturbing synapsis and sex body formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 are conclusions drawn from the comprehensive experimental data presented. The uniqueness of the model is supported by comparison to all prior work showing that other DDR mutants have pleiotropic defects.

results.result: Topbp1 null mice are embryonic lethal, TOPBP1 depletion in cell lines causes G2/M arrest and cell death, but Topbp1B5/B5 MEFs show no proliferation or DDR defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C56 are supported by citations to published work. Claim C57 is supported by the MEF data presented. Together these establish the separation-of-function nature of the B5 allele.

results.result: Other mutants with XY silencing defects (Ago4 null, Dicer CKO) show sub-fertility rather than complete sterility.
results.evaluation: Claim C58 is supported by citations to published work (Greenlee et al., 2012; Modzelewski et al., 2012). This contextualizes the severity of the Topbp1B5/B5 phenotype.

results.result: The B5 mutations disrupt TOPBP1 interactions with 53BP1 and BLM, and the TOPBP1-BLM interaction contributes to protein stabilization.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 is supported by experimental data with citations to previous reports. Claim C60 is supported by citations (Balbo Pogliano et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2013). These establish the molecular basis for the B5 allele effects.

results.result: Topbp1 CKO, Rad1 CKO, and Atr CKO spermatocytes display strong synapsis defects and defective pachytene entry, whereas Setx null spermatocytes complete autosomal synapsis while displaying MSCI defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 are supported by citations to published work (ElInati et al., 2017; Widger et al., 2018) and knowledge of Setx null phenotypes. This establishes the genetic context for interpreting the Topbp1B5/B5 phenotype.

results.result: Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes do not share all defects of Setx null spermatocytes (normal γH2AX, sumoylation, ubH2A, ATR at chromatin loops), can reach MLH1-positive crossover designation stage, and progress further in pachynema than Setx null.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C65 are based on comparison of experimental observations with published Setx phenotypes. The data support that Topbp1B5/B5 has a more limited defect than Setx null, consistent with ATR controlling specific aspects of SETX function.

results.result: R-loops affect chromatin architecture and interfere with transcription factor recruitment, highly transcribed genes accumulate more R-loops, and such genes show increased silencing defects in Topbp1B5/B5.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 are supported by citations to published work. Claim C68 is supported by experimental observations (Figure 7G). Together these support a model involving R-loop regulation in the MSCI defect.

results.result: Blm CKO mice display severe prophase I defects including incorrect pairing/synapsis and defective recombination intermediate processing leading to increased chiasmata.
results.evaluation: Claim C69 is supported by citation to published work (Holloway et al., 2010). This provides context for discussing potential BLM-related defects in Topbp1B5/B5.

results.result: MLH1 and MLH3 form a heterodimer in meiotic recombination, with MLH3 working exclusively with MLH1 while MLH1 can function with other MutL homologs.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 are supported by citations to published work (Lipkin et al., 2000; Svetlanov et al., 2008; Nakagawa et al., 1999). This provides context for interpreting the MLH1/MLH3 imbalance observed.

results.result: Short-term (4 hr) ATR inhibitor treatment causes complete loss of γH2AX, pMDC1, and SETX from XY chromosomes, and 24 hr treatment shows complete γH2AX recovery 3 hr after release.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 are supported by citations to published work (Abe et al., 2022; Sims et al., 2022). This establishes the dynamic nature of ATR signaling and MSCI maintenance.

results.result: Topbp1B5/B5 mice are viable with normal body mass and no ionizing radiation sensitivity, but display male-specific infertility with reduced testis size, complete absence of spermatozoa, increased apoptotic spermatocytes, and arrest at pachynema without progression to diplonema.
results.evaluation: All reviewers affirm the core phenotype of the Topbp1B5/B5 mouse model. Reviewer 1 states the evidence supporting 'defective maintenance of meiotic sex chromosome inactivation is solid,' and Reviewer 3 notes 'the generation of a mouse model with a very uncommon phenotype' as a main strength. No reviewer challenges these basic characterization findings.

results.result: Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes display normal pachytene entry, no gross defects in chromosome synapsis (with normal SYCP1/SYCP3 and HORMAD1/HORMAD2 patterns), reach mid-pachynema (H1t positive), and form a morphologically normal sex body.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly recognize this as a key distinguishing feature. Reviewer 1 describes the phenotype as 'defective MSCI maintenance but normal sex body formation' and notes it 'differs from that of a previous TOPBP1 null allele.' Reviewer 3 emphasizes 'despite a proper morphological formation of the sex body,' indicating acceptance of these findings.

results.result: Topbp1B5/B5 MEFs show no sensitivity to hydroxyurea or phleomycin, can activate DDR signaling (phosphorylation of CHK1, CHK2, RPA2, KAP1), recruit MDC1 to γH2AX-marked DSB foci, and show no increased micronuclei.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these somatic cell findings. The overall assessment that the mutation is a 'separation of function' affecting meiosis but not somatic DDR is accepted by all reviewers, with Reviewer 1 noting the study 'describes a TOPBP1 separation of function mutation.'

results.result: The B5 mutations disrupt TOPBP1 binding to BLM and 53BP1, and result in reduced protein levels of Flag-TOPBP1-B5 compared to wild-type.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the biochemical characterization of the B5 mutation. Reviewer 1 notes 'Additional defects in CHK phosphorylation and SETX localization are also described,' implicitly accepting the molecular characterization. No reviewer questions the interaction data.

results.result: Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes display normal DNA DSB repair (γH2AX confined to XY, RAD51 only on XY at mid-pachytene), normal TOPBP1 localization to XY chromosomes, normal localization of ATR/BRCA1/MDC1/53BP1, and mostly normal ATR signaling markers (pMDC1 T4, pCHK1 S345, pHORMAD2).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as part of the overall characterization showing separation of MSCI from other meiotic functions. Reviewer 3 notes the study shows 'despite a proper morphological formation of the sex body and the incorporation of most canonical MSCI markers,' indicating acceptance of the normal DDR marker localization.

results.result: Phosphorylation of CHK1 on S317 is significantly decreased in Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes, but this defect is unlikely to cause the observed infertility based on comparison to Chek1 CKO phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly mentions 'Additional defects in CHK phosphorylation' as part of the study's findings, accepting this observation. The interpretation that it is not causal is not challenged by any reviewer.

results.result: Phosphoproteomic analysis reveals ATR signaling is not drastically impaired in Topbp1B5/B5 testes, but SETX phosphorylation (including at S/T-Q sites) is reduced and SETX spreading to XY chromatin loops is significantly decreased.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes 'Additional defects in CHK phosphorylation and SETX localization are also described' as part of the study's findings. Reviewer 2 states 'the authors found reduced phosphorylation of a DNA/RNA helicase, Sentaxin, and decreased localization of the protein to the X-Y sex body,' explicitly affirming these results. Reviewer 3 mentions the study shows 'likely due to a defective phosphorylation of the helicase SETX.'

results.result: Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes form a sex body of grossly normal appearance with normal patterns of sex body markers (CHD4, SUMO, USP7), normal chromatin marks (H3K9ac, H3K9me3, H3K27ac, H3K36me3, H3K4me3, H4K16ac, H4ac, H2AK116ub, H3K4me1), and proper exclusion of RNA Pol2.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently recognize normal sex body formation as a key finding. Reviewer 1 describes 'defective MSCI maintenance but normal sex body formation' and Reviewer 3 notes 'despite a proper morphological formation of the sex body and the incorporation of most canonical MSCI markers.' The extensive chromatin mark analysis is not challenged.

results.result: Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals Topbp1B5/B5 testes contain only early spermatocyte populations, can initiate MSCI with robust but incomplete X chromosome silencing, but show increased X and Y gene expression in late spermatocytes including spermatocyte-toxic genes (Zfy1, Zfy2) and other MSCI marker genes (Kdm6a, Lamp2, Zfx, Uba1y, Rhox13, Scml2).
results.evaluation: All reviewers affirm the transcriptomic evidence for MSCI defects. Reviewer 2 states 'the authors also found decreased repression of several genes on the sex chromosomes in the male mice' and notes 'the works including phospho-proteomics and single-cell RNA sequencing with lots of data have been done with great care and most of the results are convincing.' The Editor states 'The evidence supporting the conclusion that the mutants display defective maintenance of meiotic sex chromosome inactivation is solid.'

results.result: During the SP2 to SP3 transition, 74 genes in Topbp1B5/B5 versus 4 in wild-type exhibit reduced silencing, while 134 genes show unaltered silencing and only 24 show increased silencing in Topbp1B5/B5 (compared to 43 unaltered and 185 increased in wild-type). The severity of silencing defects correlates with pre-leptotene RNA levels, with highly expressed genes showing more severe defects.
results.evaluation: While reviewers accept the overall MSCI defect, Reviewer 1 specifically states 'The study claims that MSCI is initiated but not maintained in the mutant. I think alternative hypotheses are possible,' suggesting uncertainty about the interpretation of the temporal dynamics of silencing. The detailed gene-by-gene analysis is not explicitly discussed by reviewers.

results.result: The Topbp1B5/B5 mouse provides a unique model uncoupling MSCI from sex body formation, representing the first DDR mutant that separates XY silencing from sex body formation and the first mutation impairing TOPBP1's meiotic silencing function without severely disturbing synapsis and sex body formation.
results.evaluation: All reviewers recognize this as the key conceptual advance. The Editor states 'This important study reports a new mutant mouse line' and emphasizes the novelty. Reviewer 1 describes it as 'a TOPBP1 separation of function mutation, resulting in defective MSCI maintenance but normal sex body formation' and notes 'The phenotype differs from that of a previous TOPBP1 null allele.' Reviewer 3 highlights 'the generation of a mouse model with a very uncommon phenotype' as a main strength.

results.result: In Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes, MLH1 foci are significantly increased while MLH3 foci numbers do not differ significantly from wild-type.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these crossover marker findings. The data are presented as part of the comprehensive characterization showing normal progression through pachynema, which reviewers accept.

results.result: Topbp1B5/B5 spermatocytes exhibit subtle defects/delays in γH2AX spreading on the PAR and pericentromeric regions, accounting for 56% of mid-pachytene cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this finding. It is presented as a minor defect consistent with the overall phenotype of largely normal sex body formation with MSCI maintenance defects, which reviewers accept.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C14-C17. Both evaluations support that somatic DDR functions are normal in the Topbp1B5/B5 model, with OpenEval citing specific experimental data (clonogenic assays, western blots, immunofluorescence) and peer reviewers accepting this as part of the separation-of-function characterization.

Perfect agreement on claims C24-C25. Both evaluations support the MLH1/MLH3 imbalance findings. OpenEval notes the functional significance cannot be determined without diplotene cells, while peer reviewers do not challenge these crossover marker findings as part of the comprehensive characterization.

Perfect agreement on claims C32-C33. Both evaluations support the reduced CHK1 phosphorylation finding. OpenEval notes C33 is an inference based on published data, while Reviewer 1 explicitly mentions CHK phosphorylation defects and accepts the interpretation that it is not causal.

Perfect agreement on claims C39-C41. Both evaluations strongly support that sex body formation and chromatin modifications are intact despite silencing defects. This is recognized by all peer reviewers as a key distinguishing feature of the model.

Agreement on claims C49-C51 with some uncertainty. OpenEval supports the detailed temporal analysis of MSCI dynamics, but Reviewer 1 specifically questions whether alternative hypotheses about MSCI initiation versus maintenance are possible, suggesting the interpretation may not be definitive.

Perfect agreement on claims C52-C54. Both evaluations strongly support that this represents a unique model separating MSCI from other meiotic functions. All peer reviewers recognize this as the key conceptual advance and main strength of the study.

Strong agreement on claims C18-C19, with peer result also covering C59. Both evaluations support the biochemical characterization of the B5 mutation and reduced ATR-TOPBP1 interaction. OpenEval notes uncertainty about exact mechanisms, while peer reviewers accept the molecular characterization without challenge.

Perfect agreement on claims C27-C28. Both evaluations support the subtle synapsis defect findings. OpenEval questions the biological significance relative to the severe phenotype, while peer reviewers accept it as a minor defect consistent with the overall phenotype.

Strong agreement on claims C4-C8, with peer result also covering C9-C11. Both evaluations support the core phenotypic characterization of the Topbp1B5/B5 model including viability, fertility defects, and meiotic arrest. All peer reviewers affirm these findings as solid.

Strong agreement on claims C29-C31, with peer result also covering C20-C21. Both evaluations support that DDR protein recruitment and canonical ATR signaling are intact. Peer reviewers accept this as evidence for separation of MSCI from other meiotic functions.

Strong agreement on claims C42-C45, with peer result also covering C46-C48. Both evaluations strongly support the scRNAseq evidence for MSCI defects. Peer reviewers emphasize the quality and care of the transcriptomic work, with the Editor stating the evidence is solid.

Strong agreement on claims C34-C35, with peer result also covering C37-C38. Both evaluations support the phosphoproteomic identification of SETX as a specific defect. Multiple peer reviewers explicitly affirm the reduced SETX phosphorylation and localization findings.

Agreement on claims C46-C48 regarding MSCI defect confirmation. OpenEval supports these claims based on scRNAseq comparison to published mutants, while peer result R9 covers these claims as part of broader transcriptomic evidence (C42-C48) that reviewers find convincing.

Strong agreement on claims C12-C13, with peer result also covering C22-C23, C26. Both evaluations support this as a key distinction from prior work showing normal synapsis completion and H1t expression despite MSCI defects. Peer reviewers explicitly recognize this separation as a distinguishing feature.

Agreement on claims C9-C11 regarding meiotic arrest at pachynema. OpenEval supports these claims with histological and cytological data, while peer result R1 covers these as part of the broader core phenotype (C4-C11) that all reviewers affirm.

Partial agreement on claims C20-C23. OpenEval supports normal progression through early prophase I including synapsis and DSB repair. Peer result R2 covers C22-C23 and C26 as part of recognizing normal sex body formation as a key distinguishing feature.

Partial agreement on claims C20-C21. OpenEval supports normal early prophase I progression, while peer result R5 covers these claims as part of broader acceptance (C20-C21, C29-C31) of normal meiotic functions separate from MSCI defects.

Agreement on claim C38 regarding SETX localization defect. OpenEval supports this with immunofluorescence including 3D-SIM data, while peer result R7 covers this as part of broader SETX findings (C34-C35, C37-C38) that multiple reviewers explicitly affirm.

Agreement on claim C59 regarding B5 mutation molecular basis. OpenEval supports this with experimental data and citations, while peer result R4 covers this as part of accepting the biochemical characterization (C18-C19, C59) of the B5 mutation.

Agreement on claim C37 regarding SETX context. OpenEval supports this with citations establishing SETX's role, while peer result R7 covers this as part of the broader SETX findings (C34-C35, C37-C38) that reviewers accept.
